name: Grande Champagne Cognac
description: The premier cru of Cognac, whose chalky soil gives a spirit so slow to mature that it is often unapproachable young and extraordinary old. Champagne here means open field, not the wine region.
funFact: The chalk is Campanian limestone, the same geology as the Champagne wine region hundreds of kilometres north, which is where the shared name comes from.

serve.how: Neat in a tulip that concentrates rather than disperses. Do not warm it in your hands — the fashion for heating cognac drives off exactly the delicate floral notes the cru is prized for.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc grown on chalk, twice pot-distilled, long-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from the Grande Champagne cru

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in Charentais pot stills

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Very long; the cru rewards decades in Limousin oak

composition.process: Rancio — the nutty, mushroomy note of great old cognac — develops here more than in any other cru.

name: Petite Champagne Cognac
description: The second cru, ringing Grande Champagne on slightly less chalky soil. Finer and faster to mature than its neighbour, and the other half of what makes a Fine Champagne blend.
funFact: A cognac labelled Fine Champagne must be Grande and Petite Champagne only, with at least half from the Grande.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature. It matures faster than Grande Champagne, so a mid-aged bottling is often more expressive than an equivalent from the premier cru at the same age.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc from the second cru, double-distilled and oak-aged.
composition.process: Slightly less chalk means slightly less structure, and a spirit that opens earlier.

name: Borderies Cognac
description: The smallest cognac cru, on clay and flint rather than chalk, producing a rounder spirit famous for violets and nuts. Only about five per cent of the region, and blenders fight over it.
funFact: At roughly 4,000 hectares it is by far the smallest of the six crus, and single-cru Borderies bottlings are correspondingly scarce.

serve.how: Neat and unwarmed. The violet note is the signature and it is fragile, so avoid ice and avoid heat. Worth tasting beside a Grande Champagne to see how much the soil does.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc on clay and flint, double-distilled and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc from the Borderies cru

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Matures faster than the Champagne crus

composition.process: Clay-flint soil rather than chalk is credited with the floral, nutty profile the cru is known for.

name: Fins Bois Cognac
description: The largest cognac cru, wrapping around all the others, giving a rounder and quicker-maturing spirit with pressed grape and stone fruit. The workhorse of most house blends.
funFact: It covers more than a third of the entire Cognac appellation, which is why it forms the backbone of most VS and VSOP blends.

serve.how: Neat, or in cocktails where its fruit-forward roundness holds up better than the finer crus. This is the cognac to use in a Sidecar without feeling guilty about it.

composition.summary: Ugni Blanc from the largest cru, double-distilled and oak-aged.
composition.process: Fast maturation makes it commercially essential, since it is drinkable years before the Champagne crus.

name: Cognac Hors d'Âge
description: Beyond age — officially the same minimum as XO, but used by houses for blends far older than any category covers. Where rancio, that nutty oxidative note, becomes the point of the drink.
funFact: The oldest components in some Hors d'Âge blends predate the phylloxera louse that destroyed the region's vineyards in the 1870s.

serve.how: Neat, in a small pour, and give it twenty minutes in the glass. Never warmed, never iced, and emphatically never mixed. The whole value is in aromas that heat destroys.

composition.summary: Very old cognac eaux-de-vie blended across decades.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Ugni Blanc, usually across several crus

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Decades; officially XO minimum but in practice far older

composition.process: Above about 50 years in cask the spirit is moved to glass demijohns to stop it taking more wood.

name: Bas-Armagnac
description: The finest of the three Armagnac zones, on sandy acidic soil in the west of Gascony. Column-distilled once to a low strength, which leaves in the character that a second pass would strip out.
funFact: Armagnac is the oldest documented distilled spirit in France, with a description of its medicinal virtues written down in 1310.

serve.how: Neat, unwarmed, in a small pour. Vintage Armagnacs are common in a way vintage cognacs are not, so buying a bottle from a birth year is genuinely possible.

composition.summary: Gascon white grapes column-distilled once and long-aged in local oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Baco, Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche, Colombard

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass through an alambic armagnaçais, to around 52%

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Black Gascon oak, often decades; vintages are common

composition.process: Single distillation to a low strength is the defining choice — it keeps congeners cognac deliberately removes.

name: Ténarèze
description: The middle Armagnac zone, on clay and limestone, giving a firmer and more structured spirit than Bas-Armagnac. Needs longer in wood, and rewards it with real grip.
funFact: Ténarèze is the zone most associated with Folle Blanche, a delicate and disease-prone grape that nearly disappeared after phylloxera.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature. Young Ténarèze can be tough going; it is a zone that genuinely needs twenty years, and blenders often use it to give backbone to softer Bas-Armagnac.

composition.summary: Gascon grapes on clay-limestone, single-distilled and long-aged.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Long ageing required; firm when young

composition.process: Clay-limestone gives structure where Bas-Armagnac's sand gives finesse.

name: Blanche Armagnac
description: Unaged Armagnac, given its own appellation only in 2005 after centuries of being drunk quietly by producers who never bottled it. Clear, floral and startlingly grape-forward.
funFact: Growers had drunk it at home for generations; it only became a legal category when the region realised there was a market for a clear, aromatic spirit.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in a small glass — treat it like an eau-de-vie rather than a brandy. It also makes an unusual and very good base for a sour, where the grape character survives citrus.

composition.summary: Gascon grapes single-distilled and rested in glass, never wood.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Folle Blanche, Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Baco

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three months in inert vessels — no wood permitted

composition.process: The rule forbidding wood is what makes it a distinct appellation rather than simply young Armagnac.

name: Calvados Pays d'Auge
description: The top Calvados appellation, twice pot-distilled from cider in the heart of Normandy. Richer and more complex than standard Calvados, and the only zone where double distillation is compulsory.
funFact: The trou normand — a shot of Calvados mid-meal to reopen the appetite — is a genuine regional custom, not a tourist invention.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or mid-meal in the Norman fashion. Older bottlings develop a dried-fruit depth that surprises people expecting apple juice. Do not chill it.

composition.summary: Norman cider twice pot-distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cider from Pays d'Auge apples, at least 70% bitter and bittersweet varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double distillation in a copper pot still, compulsory in this AOC

composition.process: Cider is fermented for weeks before distilling, which is why the base is closer to wine than to juice.

name: Calvados Domfrontais
description: The pear-driven Calvados, requiring at least 30% perry in the base — and in practice often far more. Lighter, more floral and markedly different from the apple-dominated appellations.
funFact: The perry pear trees of the Domfrontais can live over two hundred years and are often far older than the orchards' apple trees.

serve.how: Neat, slightly below room temperature so the pear stays forward. It is the Calvados to give someone who thinks they do not like Calvados — lighter and more perfumed than they expect.

composition.summary: Perry and cider column-distilled once and oak-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Minimum 30% pears; often 70% or more in practice

composition.process: Single distillation here, unlike Pays d'Auge, keeps the delicate pear aromatics intact.

name: Pommeau de Normandie
description: Fresh apple must stopped with Calvados before it can ferment, then aged in oak. Normandy's answer to Pineau des Charentes, and a far better aperitif than its obscurity suggests.
funFact: It was made informally by Norman farmers for centuries before receiving its own appellation in 1991.

serve.how: Cold, before the meal, in a small pour. It is exceptional with foie gras and with melon, and Normans also use it to deglaze pans for pork and chicken.

composition.summary: Unfermented apple must fortified with Calvados and oak-aged.

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Calvados, at least one year old

composition.process: Because fermentation never starts, the apple's own sugar is what sweetens it.

name: Macvin du Jura
description: Jura grape must fortified with the region's own marc, to a recipe recorded in the fourteenth century. Nutty and oxidative in the way everything from the Jura is.
funFact: The recipe appears in a fourteenth-century manuscript from the Abbey of Château-Chalon, which makes it one of the oldest documented fortified drinks in France.

serve.how: Cold as an aperitif or with a fruit dessert. The Jura's characteristic walnut note makes it superb with Comté, which is the local pairing and hard to improve on.

composition.summary: Jura grape must fortified with aged marc du Jura.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Must from Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard or Trousseau

components.label: Fortification
components.detail: Marc du Jura aged at least 18 months

composition.process: The marc must come from the same estate, which keeps it a genuinely local product.

name: Pisco Puro
description: Peruvian pisco from a single grape variety, distilled to proof with no water added and no wood contact. The purest expression of the category and the one that shows the grape most clearly.
funFact: Peruvian law forbids adding water after distillation, so the strength in the bottle is the strength that came off the still — a rule almost unique in world spirits.

serve.how: Cool and neat in a glass that holds aroma, or in a Pisco Sour. A puro made from Quebranta is the classic sour base; the aromatic varieties are better sipped.

composition.summary: A single permitted grape variety, fermented and distilled to bottling strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: One of eight permitted varieties, single-varietal

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper falca or alembic, distilled to proof

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three months in inert vessels; no wood

composition.process: Distilling to proof means the cut points alone determine the final strength — there is no correcting afterwards.

name: Pisco Acholado
description: A blend of grape varieties, either co-fermented or blended after distilling. Acholado means mixed, and it is the style most Peruvian bartenders reach for in a sour.
funFact: Blending is where the distiller's skill shows most, since the aromatic and non-aromatic varieties behave very differently in the glass.

serve.glass: Coupe for a sour, copita neat
serve.how: The default choice for a Pisco Sour — it has enough aromatic lift to survive lime, egg white and bitters. Neat it is more complex than a puro and less pointed.

composition.summary: Two or more permitted varieties blended, distilled to proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: A blend of aromatic and non-aromatic permitted grapes

composition.process: Blending can happen before fermentation or after distillation, and producers argue about which is better.

name: Pisco Mosto Verde
description: Distilled from must that has been stopped mid-fermentation, so sugar is still present when it hits the still. Wasteful, expensive, and produces the silkiest pisco made.
funFact: Because the must is not fully fermented, it takes substantially more grapes per bottle than any other pisco style — which is exactly why it costs more.

serve.how: Neat and cool, always. Using a mosto verde in a sour is not wrong but is close to a waste — the texture that justifies the price disappears under lime.

composition.summary: Partially fermented must distilled while sugar remains.
composition.process: Residual sugar does not survive distillation, but the unfermented must changes the aromatic profile and the mouthfeel.

name: Pisco Quebranta
description: Made from Peru's signature non-aromatic grape, a mutation of Criolla Negra that adapted to the coastal desert. Earthy and restrained rather than floral, and the traditional backbone of a Pisco Sour.
funFact: The grape is named for the way it breaks — quebrar — the palate of anyone who eats it fresh, being far too tannic for the table.

serve.glass: Copita neat, coupe in a sour
serve.how: The classic Pisco Sour base. Its lack of floral aromatics is a feature there: it gives body without fighting the lime. Neat it is a quieter, earthier pisco than the aromatic varieties.

composition.summary: Single-varietal Quebranta, fermented dry and distilled to proof.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Quebranta grapes from the Ica valley

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, single distillation to proof

composition.process: It is classed as non-aromatic, which in pisco terms means the spirit tastes of texture and earth rather than flowers.

name: Pisco Italia
description: Made from the Italia grape, a Muscat cross, and the most overtly perfumed of the Peruvian piscos. Intensely floral and grapey, and closer to a Muscat eau-de-vie than to a neutral brandy.
funFact: Italia is one of four grapes Peru classes as aromatic, alongside Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla.

serve.how: Neat and cool, in a glass wide enough to release the aromatics. It makes a striking Chilcano with ginger ale and lime, where the floral note lifts the whole drink.

composition.summary: Single-varietal Italia grapes distilled to proof.
composition.process: Aromatic varieties need gentler distillation, since the terpenes that carry the perfume are easily cooked off.

name: Brandy de Penedès
description: Catalonia's brandy, distilled from Penedès white grapes and aged by the same solera method as Jerez but in a cooler, wetter climate that slows everything down.
funFact: It holds its own protected designation separate from Brandy de Jerez, which is unusual for two brandies made in the same country by similar methods.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. It is drier and less caramel-heavy than Jerez brandy because the casks are less often ex-sherry, which makes it the better of the two in a cocktail.

composition.summary: Penedès grapes distilled and solera-aged in Catalonia.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Parellada, Macabeo and other Penedès whites

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Solera system, often in French oak rather than ex-sherry

composition.process: French oak rather than ex-sherry butts is the main reason it tastes drier than Jerez.

name: Aguardente da Lourinhã
description: Portugal's only wine-brandy appellation, from a small coastal area north of Lisbon. One of just three wine-brandy DOCs in Europe alongside Cognac and Armagnac, and by far the least known.
funFact: Cognac, Armagnac and Lourinhã are the only three demarcated wine-brandy regions in Europe, and almost nobody outside Portugal has heard of the third.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. The Atlantic climate gives high-acid base wine, which distils into something noticeably brighter than most Iberian brandy.

composition.summary: Atlantic-coast white wine distilled and oak-aged in Lourinhã.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Local white varieties from the Lourinhã DOC

composition.process: Cool Atlantic conditions give thin, acidic wine — poor to drink and excellent to distil.

name: Kanyak
description: Turkish grape brandy, made since the 1930s as part of the young republic's push to build domestic industry. Sweeter and softer than French brandy, and drunk in Turkey as often in coffee as neat.
funFact: The name is a Turkish rendering of cognac, adopted after French producers objected to the original spelling on Turkish labels.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or added to Turkish coffee. It is sweeter than western brandy, so it needs less warming and rewards a smaller pour.

composition.summary: Anatolian grapes distilled and oak-aged in Turkey.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Turkish white grapes, largely from the Aegean

composition.process: State monopoly production shaped the style for decades before privatisation.

name: Divin
description: Moldova's brandy, made by the Charentais method in a country that has grown wine grapes for four thousand years. Renamed from konyak after independence, and genuinely good for its price.
funFact: Moldova's Cricova cellars run to more than a hundred kilometres of tunnels, enough that visitors are driven through them by car.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature, and in the Moldovan manner during rather than after the meal. Older bottlings are notably soft, since local oak is milder than Limousin.

composition.summary: Moldovan white wine double-distilled and aged in local oak.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Local Moldovan oak, three years and up

composition.process: The name was coined after independence, from divine, to break with the Soviet-era konyak label.

name: Zwetschgenwasser
description: Made from the Zwetschge, a small oval damson-type plum that grows across southern Germany and Alsace. Drier and more austere than Slivovitz, and one of the classic clear fruit brandies.
funFact: The Zwetschge is a different fruit from the round Pflaume, and using the wrong one produces a noticeably jammier, less precise spirit.

serve.how: Cool but not frozen, in a small pour after a meal. The stone note is part of the character, so let it sit in the glass a minute rather than shooting it.

composition.summary: Zwetschge plums fermented whole and pot-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, tight heart cut

composition.process: A proportion of stones fermented with the fruit supplies the bitter-almond finish.

name: Mirabelle
description: Distilled from the small golden Mirabelle plum of Lorraine, which has protected status and a season lasting about six weeks. Delicate, honeyed and among the finest eaux-de-vie made.
funFact: Lorraine produces the overwhelming majority of the world's Mirabelles, and the harvest is short enough that the whole region organises around it.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a narrow glass that traps the aroma. Nose it well before drinking; a good Mirabelle smells more intensely of the fruit than the fruit does.

composition.summary: Mirabelle plums fermented and pot-distilled, unaged.
composition.process: The fruit is tiny and yields little juice, which is why good Mirabelle is priced like a fine spirit.

name: Quetsch
description: Alsatian purple plum brandy, darker and spicier in character than Mirabelle, though equally clear in the glass. Made from the same fruit family as Zwetschgenwasser across the border.
funFact: Quetsche, Zwetschge and the Slavic sliva are all the same fruit under different linguistic traditions, which is why the spirits taste like relatives.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. Alsatian restaurants pour it alongside Mirabelle and kirsch as a trio, and tasting them side by side is the best way to learn what fruit distillation does.

composition.summary: Quetsch plums fermented and double-distilled.
composition.process: More stone character than Mirabelle, which is what makes it read as spicier.

name: Himbeergeist
description: Raspberry spirit made by macerating the fruit in neutral alcohol and then redistilling, because raspberries carry too little sugar to ferment usefully on their own. Geist means spirit in exactly that sense.
funFact: Any fruit too low in sugar to ferment — raspberry, elderberry, sloe — is made as a Geist rather than a Wasser, which is a legal distinction as well as a technical one.

serve.how: Chill the glass rather than the bottle and pour a small measure. The aroma is the entire product. It is also superb poured over fresh raspberries as a dessert.

composition.summary: Raspberries macerated in neutral spirit, then redistilled.
composition.process: Fermenting raspberries directly gives almost no alcohol, hence the maceration-and-redistill method.

name: Vieille Prune
description: Plum brandy aged in oak until it turns amber — the aged counterpart to the clear plum eaux-de-vie, and a speciality of southwest France. Softer and rounder, with the fruit turned to compote.
funFact: Souillac in the Lot has made it for centuries, and older bottlings can spend twenty years or more in cask before release.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner. Unlike clear plum brandy this one takes warmth well and behaves more like an Armagnac than an eau-de-vie.

composition.summary: Plums fermented, distilled and aged in oak for years.

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak casks, often a decade or more

composition.process: Wood ageing turns the sharp stone-fruit character into something closer to dried fruit and spice.

name: Eau-de-Vie de Coing
description: Quince brandy, from a fruit that is hard, astringent and nearly inedible raw but distils into one of the most perfumed spirits in the category. Difficult to make and made in small quantities.
funFact: Quince yields very little juice for its weight and ferments slowly, which is why quince eau-de-vie is among the most expensive fruit distillates.

serve.how: Cool and neat, in a small pour, at the end of a meal. It is intensely floral and does not need help. Alsatian producers make it in tiny runs and it sells out locally.

composition.summary: Quinces fermented whole and pot-distilled.
composition.process: The fruit must be fully ripe and yellow; green quince gives a harsh, resinous spirit.

name: Holunderbeergeist
description: Elderberry spirit, made by maceration and redistillation like Himbeergeist because the berries carry too little sugar to ferment. Dark-fruited and faintly tannic, quite unlike elderflower.
funFact: Elderberries are mildly toxic raw and must be processed, which is one reason the spirit is far less common than the flower liqueur.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. It is darker and more brooding than the pale fruit spirits, and works well after game or a rich stew rather than a light dessert.

composition.summary: Elderberries macerated in neutral spirit and redistilled.
composition.process: Distillation removes the compounds that make raw elderberries unwise to eat.

name: Eau-de-Vie de Sorbier
description: Rowan berry spirit from the Alps and central Europe, made from a fruit so bitter that it must be frosted on the tree before it is usable. One of the rarest eaux-de-vie in production.
funFact: Rowan berries need a hard frost to break down their sorbic acid, so the harvest cannot begin until the first serious cold snap.

serve.how: Cool and neat in a small pour. It is astringent and unusual, and it belongs at the end of a long meal rather than as an introduction to fruit brandy.

composition.summary: Frosted rowan berries fermented and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Sorbic acid, named for this genus, is what makes the raw fruit unusable until frost breaks it down.
